The cylinder was oriented both perpendicular and parallel to its long axis as it moved, and we found that the drag it experienced differed significantly in the two orientations, a phenomenon we call anisotropy. This anisotropy varied greatly with the speed at which the cylinder was moved, its length compared to its width, and whether the grains it was moving through had high friction or little friction. Notably, the anisotropy increased more quickly in beds with low friction. Additionally, the drag experienced by the cylinder was found to be influenced more by its long axis than its ends. This phenomenon could be understood by studying the flow of sediment around the cylinder and estimating the drag experienced by its sides and flat ends. This estimation confirmed that the anisotropy of the drag could be explained by the different shapes of the areas surrounding the cylinder's sides and ends, and how these shapes changed as the cylinder moved. Furthermore, the research found that the flow of the granular material could be modelled by a simplified two-dimensional simulation. The study also compared the drag experienced by the cylinder in the granular material to the drag it would experience in a fluid, revealing both similarities and differences, with the anisotropy of the drag being one of the former. The research could have implications for understanding how animals that move through loose sediments move themselves. The code used

Researchers have a rich history of developing and analyzing preservation-based discretization techniques, including validating existing schemes' preservation properties and proposing innovative methods achieving both high accuracy and property preservation. Two alternatives, Wavefield Reconstruction Inversion (WRI) and Extended Source Waveform Inversion (ESI), have been proposed as methods to overcome this limitation. Both of these methods break the non-linear link between wavefields and model parameters by utilizing wavefields as intermediate variables, thus ensuring that the solution to ESI or WRI is equivalent to the minimum of FWI. We compare the performance of these three methods on synthetic data sets, specifically 2D and 3D models with noisy data, and also investigate the pre-conditioning effect of initial models on these methods. Our results show that the three methods all converge to the same solution, with the quality of the initial model playing a crucial role in their success, especially for the 3D case. In this study, we used a two-dimensional radiative hydrodynamic model to thoroughly examine the effects of laser energy and wavelength on the formation of plasma within biological tissue, with a particular focus on the optical properties that allow for accurate interpretation of LIBS data. Our research simulated the process of laser-induced plasma formation in detail and demonstrated how the optical signals that immediately follow the laser pulse quickly stabilize over time, with little variation among different wavelengths of the laser. In contrast, the duration of plasma existence was found to significantly depend on the depth of the target tissue, with deeper tissues requiring more time to extinguish, but showed little correlation with laser energy or wavelength, and had a more significant impact on the composition of the plasma. Consequently, our findings suggest that the wavelength of the laser has limited influence on the analytical capabilities of LIBS, and that deeper tissues may pose a greater challenge, with a possible need for more powerful lasers to penetrate these areas with minimal tissue damage. Moreover, our research implies that the temporal analysis of LIBS signals could be valuable in determining the depth of the target tissue, with a possible indicator of the duration of plasma existence that is directly proportional to the depth of the tissue

Current mapping approaches rely heavily on state separation principles, which can limit the versatility of maps and impose strict navigation constraints. To address this limitation, this paper introduces Dynamic SLAM, a robust algorithm capable of integrating multiple separated submaps into a unified map structure. By doing so, it generates a single, navigable representation of the environment that lacks artificial boundaries. A Mach-Zehnder atomic interferometry system can be employed to sensitively detect these minuscule magnetic fields.
